Kassapa Chapter Santuṭṭha Sutta: Contented At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there is one person who arises in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. Who is that one person? It is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. This is that one person who arises in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. “Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will be content with any kind of robe; we will be content with any kind of almsfood; we will be content with any kind of lodging; we will be content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. Thus should you train yourselves. When this was said, the Venerable Mahākassapa said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There is one person who arises in the world for the welfare of many… for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. “Venerable sir, I too am one who is content with any kind of robe, content with any kind of almsfood, content with any kind of lodging, and content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. “It is wonderful, Kassapa, it is marvelous! You have attained the same state of contentment as I have. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will be content with any kind of robe… we will be content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. Thus should you train yourselves. When this was said, the Venerable Mahākassapa said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There is one person who arises in the world for the welfare of many… for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. “Venerable sir, I am one who is content with any kind of robe, content with any kind of almsfood, content with any kind of lodging, and content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. But, venerable sir, there is another person who is even more content than I am. “Who, Kassapa, is that other person who is even more content than you? “Venerable sir, it is the bhikkhu who dwells in the forest, who eats only what is left over from his almsround, who wears rag-robes, who is a refuse-rag wearer, who is a three-rober, who is a one-session eater, who eats only from the bowl, who does not eat after the time, who is a forest-dweller, who is a tree-root dweller, who is a open-air dweller, who is a chaff-fire dweller, who is a any-bed-user, who is a sitter, who is a one-sitter, who is a never-lying-downer, who is a water-drinker, who is an eater of greens, who is an eater of jujube fruits, who is an eater of wild rice, who is an eater of water hyacinth roots, who is an eater of lotus roots, who is an eater of sesamum seeds, who is an eater of rice bran, who is an eater of rice-scum, who is an eater of grass, who is an eater of cow dung, who is an eater of rice-water, who is an eater of moss, who is a gleaner, who is a refuse-eater, who is a forest-dweller, who is a tree-root dweller, who is a open-air dweller, who is a chaff-fire dweller, who is a any-bed-user, who is a sitter, who is a one-sitter, who is a never-lying-downer, who is a water-drinker, who is an eater of greens, who is an eater of jujube fruits, who is an eater of wild rice, who is an eater of water hyacinth roots, who is an eater of lotus roots, who is an eater of sesamum seeds, who is an eater of rice bran, who is an eater of rice-scum, who is an eater of grass, who is an eater of cow dung, who is an eater of rice-water, who is an eater of moss, who is a gleaner, who is a refuse-eater.

He is the one who is even more content than I am. “It is wonderful, Kassapa, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by you: ‘Venerable sir, it is the bhikkhu who dwells in the forest… who is a refuse-eater. He is the one who is even more content than I am. “Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will be content with any kind of robe… we will be content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. Thus should you train yourselves. When this was said, the Venerable Mahākassapa said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There is one person who arises in the world for the welfare of many… for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. “Venerable sir, I am one who is content with any kind of robe, content with any kind of almsfood, content with any kind of lodging, and content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. And there is that other person who is even more content than I am. But, venerable sir, there is yet another person who is even more content than both of us. “Who, Kassapa, is that other person who is even more content than both you and him? “Venerable sir, it is the bhikkhu who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling. He is the one who is even more content than both of us. “It is wonderful, Kassapa, it is marvelous! But, venerable sir, there is yet another person who is even more content than all of us. “Who, Kassapa, is that other person who is even more content than all of us? “Venerable sir, it is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. How well this has been stated by you: ‘Venerable sir, it is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Thus should you train yourselves. When this was said, the Venerable Mahākassapa said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There is one person who arises in the world for the welfare of many… for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. “Venerable sir, I am one who is content with any kind of robe, content with any kind of almsfood, content with any kind of lodging, and content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. And there is that other person who is even more content than all of us. At Sāvatthī.
“Monks, this Kassapa is content with whatever robe he receives, and he speaks in praise of being content with whatever robe one receives.

He does not engage in improper search for the sake of a robe; if he does not obtain a robe, he is not distressed; and having obtained a robe, he uses it without clinging, without infatuation, without attachment, seeing the danger in it and understanding the escape from it.
"Monks, this Kassapa is content with whatever almsfood he receives, and he speaks in praise of being content with whatever almsfood one receives.
He does not resort to improper search for the sake of almsfood; if he does not obtain almsfood, he is not distressed;
and if he obtains almsfood, he is unattached, uninfatuated, and unaddicted to it, seeing the danger in it."
He enjoys [requisites] with wisdom regarding escape.
Monks, this Kassapa is content with whatever kind of lodging he receives, and he speaks in praise of being content with whatever lodging one receives;
yet, for the sake of a lodging, he does not engage in improper search, nor does he fail to obtain a lodging.

He does not become agitated; and having obtained a lodging, he uses it without attachment, without infatuation, and without being consumed by passion, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape.
Monks, this Kassapa is content with whatever medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive.
He speaks in praise of contentment with whatever medicinal requisites for the sick are available from various sources;
he does not engage in improper or unsuitable search for the sake of medicinal requisites for the sick;
he is not anxious if he does not obtain such requisites; and having obtained them, he is unattached, uninfatuated, and undeluded, seeing the danger therein.
One who possesses the wisdom of escape makes use [of requisites].

Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: “We will be content with whatever robe we obtain, and we will speak in praise of being content with whatever robe one obtains. We will not engage in improper search for the sake of a robe.

If we do not obtain a robe, we will not be distressed. And if we do obtain a robe, we will use it without attachment, without infatuation, without being consumed by it, seeing the danger in it and possessing the wisdom of escape.”
(Thus all should be done.
“We shall be content with whatever almsfood we receive … [and so on] … we shall be content with whatever lodging we receive … [and so on].”
We shall be content with whatever medicinal requisites for the sick we may receive, and we shall speak in praise of being content with whatever medicinal requisites for the sick one may receive.

We shall not engage in improper or unsuitable searches for the sake of medicinal requisites for the sick, and having failed to obtain such requisites, we shall not be anxious; and having obtained medicinal requisites for the sick, [we shall remain content].

“‘We shall consume [food] without being intoxicated, without being infatuated, without being addicted, seeing the danger, and with wisdom regarding the escape’—in this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
For I will either exhort you by means of Kassapa, or someone who is like Kassapa; and once exhorted, you must practice accordingly.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 16.2 (SN 16.2, PTS SN ii 195) 1.
Kassapa Chapter
The Discourse on Lack of Moral Dread.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Venerable Mahākassapa and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahākassapa. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākassapa.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa:

“It is said here, friend Kassapa: ‘One who is not ardent and lacks a sense of moral dread is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage;
but one who is ardent and possesses a sense of moral dread is capable of enlightenment, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.

To what extent, friend, is one not ardent and lacking a sense of moral dread, being incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, and incapable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage?”
“And to what extent, friends, is one ardent and possessed of moral dread, capable of awakening, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage?
“In this case, friends, a bhikkhu does not apply ardor, thinking: ‘If unarisen evil, unwholesome states were to arise in me, they would lead to my harm,’ nor does he think:
‘If arisen evil, unwholesome states are not abandoned by me, they will lead to my harm.’”
He does not exert himself with the thought, "If unarisen wholesome states do not arise in me, it will lead to my harm";
he does not exert himself with the thought, "If arisen wholesome states cease in me, it will lead to my harm.
In this way, friend, one is without ardor.
And how, friends, is one lacking moral dread? Here, friends, a bhikkhu does not feel moral dread at the thought:

"If unarisen evil, unwholesome states were to arise in me, they would lead to my harm," nor does he feel moral dread at the thought: "If arisen evil, unwholesome states are not abandoned by me, they will lead to my harm."
He does not feel dread at the thought, “Unarisen wholesome states might fail to arise, which would lead to my harm”;
he does not feel dread at the thought, “Arisen wholesome states might cease, which would lead to my harm.
In this way, friend, one is without dread.
"In this way, friend, one who is without ardor and without fear of wrongdoing is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.
And how, friend, is one ardent?
Here, friend, a bhikkhu thinks: 'If unarisen evil, unwholesome states were to arise in me, they would lead to my harm.'"
He exerts himself with ardor, thinking: "If these evil, unwholesome states that have arisen in me are not abandoned, they will lead to my harm.
He exerts himself with ardor: "May wholesome states that have not yet arisen in me [arise]... and so on; he exerts himself with ardor.
In this way, friend, one is ardent.
And how, friends, is one conscientious?

Here, friends, a bhikkhu is conscientious, thinking: "If unarisen evil, unwholesome states were to arise in me, they would lead to my harm," and "If arisen evil, unwholesome states were not abandoned by me, they would lead to my harm."
One feels dread at the thought, "Unarisen wholesome states, if they do not arise, might lead to my harm";
one feels dread at the thought, "Arisen wholesome states, if they cease, might lead to my harm.
It is in this way, friend, that one is possessed of moral dread.
“It is in this way, friends, that one who is ardent and possessed of moral dread is capable of self-awakening, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.
The second [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 16.3 (SN 16.3, PTS SN ii 197)
1. The Chapter on Kassapa. The Discourse on the Simile of the Moon.
[The Blessed One] was staying at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, approach families like a moon—
drawing back both body and mind, always fresh among families, and free from arrogance. Just as, monks,
a man might look down into an old well, or a mountain precipice, or a river gorge.”
With body withdrawn and mind withdrawn,
in this very way, monks, you should approach families like the moon—
with body withdrawn and mind withdrawn, ever-new among families, and free from arrogance.
“Bhikkhus, Kassapa approaches families like the moon—
keeping his body withdrawn, keeping his mind withdrawn, ever-new to families, and free from arrogance.
What do you think, bhikkhus?”
“What kind of bhikkhu is worthy of approaching families?
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”
Then the Blessed One waved his hand in the air:
"Just as, monks, this hand in the air does not stick, is not grasped, and is not bound, even so, monks,
for whatever monk approaches families, if his mind does not stick, is not grasped, and is not bound among those families..."
‘May those who desire gain obtain it; may those who desire merit perform meritorious deeds.
Just as he is pleased and glad at his own gain, so too is he pleased and glad at the gain of others.
It is such a bhikkhu, monks, who is worthy to visit families.
Monks, when Kassapa approaches families, his mind does not cling, become attached, or become bound among them with the thought:
"May those who desire gain obtain it; may those who desire merit perform meritorious deeds.
He is content and glad at heart with whatever gain he receives for himself.
Thus, one is glad and joyful at the gain of others.
What do you think, monks,
what kind of monk’s teaching of the Dhamma is impure, and what kind of monk’s teaching of the Dhamma is pure?”
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“In that case, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to others with such a thought as this: ‘May they understand my meaning; may they grasp my meaning’—he is one who teaches the Dhamma to others with a mind that is not rightly directed.”
‘Oh, that they might hear my Dhamma! And having heard the Dhamma, may they have confidence in it!
And being confident, may they manifest their confidence toward me!’—for a monk with such a mind, monks, the teaching of the Dhamma is unpurified.
But when a monk teaches the Dhamma to others with this intention:
‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One—it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves.
“Oh, may they hear the Dhamma! Having heard the Dhamma, may they understand it! Having understood it, may they practice accordingly!
Thus, relying on the excellence of the Dhamma, he teaches the Dhamma to others; out of compassion, out of sympathy, and out of pity, he teaches the Dhamma to others.
“Monks, for a monk such as this, the teaching of the Dhamma is perfectly pure.
Kassapa, monks, teaches the Dhamma to others with this intention:
‘The Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be realized by the wise for themselves.’”
“Oh, that they might hear my Dhamma! Having heard the Dhamma, may they understand it! And having understood it, may they practice accordingly!
Thus, out of regard for the excellence of the Dhamma, he teaches the Dhamma to others; out of compassion, out of sympathy, and out of pity, he teaches the Dhamma to others.
“Bhikkhus, I shall exhort you with Kassapa, or with one who is like Kassapa; and when you have been exhorted, you must practice accordingly.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 16.4 (SN 16.4, PTS SN ii 200) 1.
Kassapa Chapter
The Discourse on the Hermitage.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying. “What do you think, bhikkhus?”
“In what manner is a bhikkhu worthy to be a family visitor, and in what manner is a bhikkhu not worthy to be a family visitor?
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One...
[as before] ... The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu approaches families with such a thought as this:
‘May they give to me, may they not not give;
may they give much to me, may they not give little;’”
"Let them give me only what is excellent, not what is coarse;
let them give me quickly, not slowly;
let them give me respectfully, not disrespectfully."
If, monks, when that bhikkhu approaches families with such a mind, they do not give, he is disappointed by that; on account of that, he experiences pain and mental distress.
They give little, not much...
they give coarse food, not fine food...
They give slowly, not quickly; because of that, the bhikkhu is offended, and on that account he experiences pain and mental distress.
They give without respect, not with respect; because of that, the bhikkhu is offended, and on that account he experiences pain and mental distress.
Such a bhikkhu, monks, is not worthy to be a visitor of families.
But, monks, that monk who approaches families with such a thought as this:
"How could it be obtained from other families here—
that they should give to me, and not fail to give?"
"Let them give me much, not little;
let them give me what is refined, not coarse;
let them give me quickly, not slowly."
"Let them give to me respectfully, not disrespectfully.
If, monks, while that bhikkhu approaches families with such a thought, they do not give, the bhikkhu is not offended; he does not experience pain or mental distress on that account.
If they give little, not much, the bhikkhu is not offended; he does not experience pain or mental distress on that account.
They give what is coarse, not what is refined; because of that, the bhikkhu is not offended; he does not experience suffering and mental distress on that account.
They give slowly, not quickly; because of that, the bhikkhu is not offended; he does not experience suffering and mental distress on that account.
They give without respect, not with respect; because of that, the bhikkhu is not offended; he does not experience suffering and mental distress on that account.
“Monks, such a monk as this is worthy to be a visitor to families.
Kassapa approaches families with this thought:
‘How could one possibly obtain anything from other families?’”
"Let them give me only what is sufficient, not too little;
let them give me much, not a small amount;
let them give me only what is excellent, not what is coarse."
"May they give to me quickly, not slowly;
may they give to me respectfully, not disrespectfully.
But if, monks, while Kassapa approaches families with such a mind, they do not give, Kassapa is not offended by it; he does not experience suffering or mental distress on that account.
They give little, not much; because of that, Kassapa is not displeased, and he does not experience suffering or mental distress on that account.
They give coarse food, not refined; because of that, Kassapa is not displeased, and he does not experience suffering or mental distress on that account.
They give slowly, not quickly; because of that, Kassapa is not displeased, and he does not experience suffering or mental distress on that account.
“They give without respect, not with respect; therefore Kassapa is not offended. Because of that, he does not experience pain and mental distress.
Whether it be by Kassapa, monks, or by one who is like Kassapa, that you should advise me—having been advised, you must practice accordingly.

The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what now is aging-and-death, and for whom is there this aging-and-death? “Any kind of form whatsoever, bhikkhu, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called ‘form. Any kind of consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called ‘consciousness. “Venerable Kassapa, it was for three reasons that the Blessed One prescribed eating in groups of three among families:

for the restraint of ill-behaved persons, for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus, so that those with evil desires might not break the Saṅgha by taking a faction, and out of compassion for families.
It was for these three reasons, venerable Kassapa, that the Blessed One prescribed eating in groups of three among families.”

“Now why, friend Ānanda, do you wander on tour together with these new bhikkhus who do not guard the doors of their sense faculties, who are immoderate in eating, and who are not devoted to wakefulness?
It seems to me you are wandering about destroying crops; it seems to me you are wandering about destroying families.
Your retinue, friend Ānanda, is falling apart.”
“Friends, those new shoots are indeed decaying.
This young man has not known moderation.
“Venerable Kassapa, gray hairs have even grown upon my head.”
"And yet, even today, we have not escaped the charge of being called 'children' by the Venerable Mahākassapa.

"For indeed, friend Ānanda, you are wandering on tour together with these young bhikkhus who do not guard the doors of their sense faculties, who are immoderate in eating, and who are not devoted to wakefulness; it is as if you were trampling down a crop of grain!"
"You are acting, friend Ānanda, as one who destroys his own family; I think you are acting as one who destroys his own family.
Your assembly is falling apart, friend Ānanda; your new recruits are falling away."
“Or perhaps this young man did not realize his own measure.
Then the nun Thullanandā heard:
“It seems that the venerable Mahākassapa has disparaged the venerable Ānanda Vedehamuni by calling him a ‘young man.’”
Then the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, being displeased, uttered these words of displeasure:
"How can the noble Mahākassapa, having formerly been a follower of another sect, think it right to disparage the noble Ānanda, the sage of Videha, with the address 'young boy'?
The Venerable Mahākassapa heard the bhikkhunī Thullanandā speaking these words.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Truly, friend Ānanda, the nun Thullanandā spoke these words rashly and without reflection.
For when I, friend, having shaved off my hair and beard and donned the saffron robes, went forth from the home life into homelessness..."
Having gone forth, I do not recall having acknowledged any other teacher than that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Formerly, friends, when I was still a householder, this thought occurred to me:
"The life of a householder is cramped, a path of dust; going forth is the open air."
"It is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) that is entirely complete, entirely pure, and polished like a conch shell.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?

Then, friends, after some time, having had a robe made of patchwork rags, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness, directed toward those who are Worthy Ones (arahants) in the world.
Having thus gone forth, while traveling along the highway, I saw the Blessed One seated at the Bahuputta Shrine between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā.
Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to me:
“May I see the Teacher! May I see the Blessed One himself!”
“If I were to see the Sugata, I would indeed see the Blessed One;
if I were to see the Perfectly Enlightened One,
I would indeed see the Blessed One.”
Then, friends, right there I prostrated myself with my head at the Blessed One’s feet and said this to the Blessed One:
“The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.
The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.”
When this was said, friends, the Blessed One said this to me:
“Kassapa, if anyone were to say of a disciple who is thus endowed with all his faculties that he knows when he does not know, or that he sees when he does not see, his head would split apart.
But as for me, Kassapa, I say that I know only what I know, and I say that I see only what I see.”
Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus:
"Strong shame and fear of wrongdoing shall be established in me toward elders, juniors, and those of middle standing.
In this way, Kassapa, should you train yourself.
Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus:
"Whatever teaching I hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will listen to it all with intentness, attending to it with my mind, applying my whole heart, and lending an attentive ear.
In this way, Kassapa, should you train yourself.
Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus:
"May mindfulness directed to the body, accompanied by pleasure, not be abandoned by me.
In this way, Kassapa, should you train yourself.
Then, friends, after the Blessed One had exhorted me with this instruction, he rose from his seat and departed.
For seven days, friends, I ate the country alms-food while still a seeker; on the eighth day, final knowledge arose.
Then, friends, the Blessed One, having stepped down from the path, approached the foot of a certain tree.
Then, friends, having spread out my outer robe made of patches of cloth folded fourfold, I said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One sit here; may it be for my long-term welfare and happiness.
The Blessed One, friends, sat down on the prepared seat.
When I had sat down, friend, the Blessed One said this to me:
“This outer robe made of patchwork rags from a dust-heap is indeed soft for you, Kassapa.
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my outer robe made of patchwork rags out of compassion,” I said.
"But will you wear for me, Kassapa, these worn-out hempen rag-robes?
"I shall wear them, Bhante, these worn-out hempen rag-robes of the Blessed One.
And so, friend, I gave the Blessed One my outer robe made of pieces of coarse cloth.
But I, friend, accepted from the Blessed One those worn-out hempen rag-robes.

For if one were speaking rightly, friend, of anyone who could be called "the Blessed One’s legitimate son, born of his breast, born of his mouth, born of the Dhamma, created by the Dhamma, an heir to the Dhamma," it is of me that one would rightly say: "He has accepted those worn-out hempen rag-robes."
‘He is the Blessed One’s own son, born from his mouth, born of the Dhamma, created by the Dhamma, an heir to the Dhamma; he has accepted hempen rags, refuse-rags, and discarded robes.

And I, friend, as long as I wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
And I, friend, as long as I wish... [and so on].
(The detailed exposition of the nine successive dwellings in attainment and the five direct knowledges should be understood in this way:

"Friends, having realized for myself through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through the destruction of the taints, I dwell having attained them.

Friend, one might think that a seven-cubit or seven-and-a-half-cubit elephant could be concealed by a palm leaf; yet one who would think that my six direct knowledges could be concealed is like that."
And yet the bhikkhunī Thullanandā has fallen away from the holy life.
The eleventh.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 16.12 (SN 16.12, PTS SN ii 222).
1. The Chapter on Kassapa. Sutta on Death:
At one time the Venerable Mahākassapa and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahākassapa. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākassapa.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa:
"Friend Kassapa, does the Tathāgata exist after death?"
“Friend, this has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
‘Does the Tathāgata exist after death?
“But then, friend, does the Tathāgata not exist after death?”
“Thus, friend, it has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
‘A Tathāgata does not exist after death.
“Then, friend, does a Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death?”
“Friend, this has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.
“But then, friend, has it been declared that ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?”
“Thus, friend, it was left undeclared by the Blessed One:
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
“And why, friend, was this left undeclared by the Blessed One?”
“Friend, this is not conducive to welfare, nor is it fundamental to the holy life; it does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.
Therefore, it was left undeclared by the Blessed One.
“But then, friend, what was declared by the Blessed One?”
“‘This is suffering,’ friend, has been declared by the Blessed One;
‘this is the origin of suffering’ has been declared by the Blessed One;
‘this is the cessation of suffering’ has been declared by the Blessed One.”
“This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,” thus it was declared by the Blessed One.
“And why, friend, was this declared by the Blessed One?

“Because, friend, this is beneficial, this pertains to the fundamentals of the holy life; this leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.”
“Therefore, that was declared by the Blessed One.
The twelfth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 16.13 (SN 16.13, PTS SN ii 223)
1. The Chapter on Kassapa:
The Discourse on Counterfeit True Dhamma.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahākassapa said this to the Blessed One:
“What, Bhante, is the cause, what is the reason, why formerly there were fewer training rules and yet more bhikkhus established themselves through direct knowledge?”
“But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why nowadays there are more training rules and fewer bhikkhus who stand firm in their knowledge?
“It is so, Kassapa. When beings are declining and the true Dhamma is disappearing, there are more training rules and fewer bhikkhus who stand firm in their knowledge.
The disappearance of the true Dhamma does not take place, Kassapa, as long as a counterfeit of the true Dhamma has not arisen in the world.”
But when, Kassapa, a counterfeit of the true Dhamma arises in the world, then the disappearance of the true Dhamma occurs.
Just as, Kassapa, there is no disappearance of gold so long as a counterfeit of gold has not arisen in the world;
but when, Kassapa, a counterfeit of gold arises in the world, then the disappearance of gold occurs.
In the same way, Kassapa, the true Dhamma does not disappear as long as a counterfeit of the true Dhamma has not arisen in the world.
But when a counterfeit of the true Dhamma arises in the world, then the true Dhamma disappears.

It is not the earth element, Kassapa, that causes the true Dhamma to disappear; it is not the water element; it is not the fire element; it is not the air element that causes the true Dhamma to disappear.
Rather, it is right here that those foolish men arise who cause this true Dhamma to disappear.
Just as a ship might sink from the very beginning,
Kassapa, such is not how the disappearance of the true Dhamma occurs.
"Kassapa, there are these five conditions that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
What are the five?
Here, Kassapa, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Teacher."
They dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Dhamma; they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Saṅgha;
they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the training; they dwell without reverence and without deference toward concentration.
These, Kassapa, are the five things that lead to the decline and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
"Kassapa, there are these five things that lead to the stability, the non-confusion, and the non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
What are the five?
Here, Kassapa, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen dwell with reverence for the Teacher."
“They dwell with deference, Kassapa, being respectful toward the Dhamma; they dwell with deference, being respectful toward the Saṅgha;
they dwell with deference, being respectful toward the training; they dwell with deference, being respectful toward concentration.
These, Kassapa, are the five qualities that lead to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.”
The Thirteenth.
The First Chapter on Kassapa.
Its summary verse:
One who is contented yet lacks moral dread,
who frequents families like the moon,
who is aged, and the three kinds of advice.
Meditative absorption and direct knowledge as one's dwelling;
robes as the state after death;
and the counterfeit of the true Dhamma.
The Connected Discourses on Kassapa are complete.
